183.title: A lamp to my feet (Psalm 118 [119]:105)
183.hook: thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths
183.carry: enough light for the next step
183.howItsDone: Many Catholics memorize Psalm 118 [119]:105 and pray it before reading scripture; it is sung in the Liturgy of the Hours and often quoted at the start of Bible study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the alphabet psalm: twenty-two stanzas, one for every Hebrew letter. Your line was a to z of love. Today we open that long psalm at a single verse. Day one hundred eighty-three.

You get up in the night for a glass of water. The house is dark. You don't turn on every light in the building. You pick up your phone, tap the little flashlight, and point it at the floor. It shows you about three steps. The edge of the rug. The corner of the table. The doorway. That's all. And it's enough, because you don't need to see the kitchen from the bedroom. You only need to see the next step, and then the one after that. Three thousand years ago, a poet had the same thought. Today: a lamp to my feet.
screen: `A DARK HOUSE AT NIGHT.` → `A LIGHT FOR THREE STEPS.` → `AND IT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: The verse sits in the middle of yesterday's alphabet psalm, at the start of the stanza for the letter nun. In the Douay-Rheims: "Thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths." First, picture the lamp. It isn't a streetlight or a lighthouse. In ancient Israel a lamp was a small clay dish, the size of your palm, with olive oil and a wick. The Hebrew word is ner. Hold one up at night and it lights a small circle around your feet. That's the point. The psalmist isn't promising a floodlight over the whole road. He's saying God's word lights the next step. Second, notice what it doesn't promise. It doesn't say you'll see the map. It doesn't say you'll know where the road bends next year. Most people want the whole route before they start walking. The psalm offers something smaller and steadier: enough light to walk by. Third, why that's comfort and not a letdown. If you could see the whole road, you might not need a lamp at all, or a hand to hold. A small light keeps you close to the one who holds it. Catholics hear God's word here in two senses: the scriptures they read, and the Word made flesh, Christ, whom Saint John calls the light. Jews hear it as the Torah, the teaching that guides daily life. Both read the same verse, and both hear the same promise: not everything, just enough.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one verse before you walk out. Settle, and breathe. Think of the next thing you'll walk into today: a room, a meeting, a hard conversation, a school gate. Don't plan the whole day. Just see the doorway. If you pray, say the verse slowly: thy word is a lamp to my feet, and a light to my paths. If you don't, simply ask yourself what the next right step is, only the next one. The bell holds the time.
A lamp to my feet. A small light held low, showing the next step and not the whole road. Today's word.
screen: `A LAMP TO MY FEET — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: enough light for the next step. Today, when you feel you can't see how something ends, stop asking for the map and take the one step you can see. Day one hundred eighty-three.

184.title: Songs of the road (Psalm 120 [121])
184.hook: pilgrims climbing to Jerusalem sang these: I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains
184.howItsDone: Catholics pray the gradual psalms (Psalms 119–133 [120–134]) in the Liturgy of the Hours, especially at the midday hour, and Psalm 120 [121] is often prayed for travelers and at funerals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a lamp to my feet. Your line was enough light for the next step. What step did you take without seeing the whole road? Today, the road itself. Day one hundred eighty-four.

Think of a long car trip with family. Somewhere around the second hour, somebody starts a song, and everybody knows the words, and the miles go faster. Now picture that on foot. Families walking for days toward Jerusalem for the great feasts, grandparents, kids, neighbors from the same village. The last stretch is uphill all the way, because Jerusalem sits high in the hills. And as they climbed, they sang. The Psalter kept their road songs, fifteen of them in a row. Today: the gradual psalms.
screen: `A SONG ON A LONG TRIP.` → `FAMILIES WALKING TO JERUSALEM.` → `UPHILL, SINGING.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Fifteen psalms in a row each carry the same heading. In Hebrew it's shir ha-ma'alot, a song of the goings up. In the Latin Bible it became canticum graduum, a song of the steps, and so the Douay-Rheims calls each one a gradual canticle. Gradual has nothing to do with slowly here. It comes from the Latin gradus, a step. Many English Bibles call them the Songs of Ascents. Second, the steps. Nobody knows for certain why they got the name. Many think it's the climb up to Jerusalem. An old Jewish tradition, written down in the Mishnah, says the Levites sang on fifteen steps in the Temple, one song for each step. Either way, these are songs for people on the move, going up. Third, today's psalm, the most loved of them. In the Douay-Rheims: "I have lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from whence help shall come to me. My help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth." Imagine a pilgrim looking up at the hills, a long climb ahead. Where does help come from? Not from the hills. From the one who made them. Then the psalm promises: "Behold he shall neither slumber nor sleep, that keepeth Israel." On the road you sleep in the open, and someone has to keep watch. The psalm says someone is. Catholics still pray the gradual psalms in the Liturgy of the Hours, and this one is often prayed for travelers, and at funerals, for the last journey.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up at something high. A tree, a rooftop, a hill, the ceiling, the sky through a window. Settle your breathing and let your eyes rest there. Think of the climb in front of you this week. Name it. Then, if you pray, say the line: my help is from the Lord, who made heaven and earth. If you don't, just stay with the looking up, and let your shoulders drop. The bell holds the time.
Gradual psalms. From the Latin for steps: fifteen songs sung by people going up to Jerusalem. Today's word.
Your line: help comes. Today, when a task looks like a hill, look up for a moment before you start the climb. Day one hundred eighty-four.

185.title: I rejoiced (Psalm 121 [122])
185.hook: let us go into the house of the Lord; pray for the peace of Jerusalem
185.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 121 [122] in the Liturgy of the Hours, often at Vespers on feasts of Mary, and its first verse, Laetatus sum, is sung at the entrance of Mass on the Fourth Sunday of Lent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the gradual psalms, songs for the climb to Jerusalem. Your line was help comes. What hill did you look up at? Today, the pilgrims arrive. Day one hundred eighty-five.

You know the feeling when someone says, let's go. Let's go to the beach. Let's go see Grandma. Let's go to the game. Before you've moved an inch, something in you is already smiling. The trip starts in the invitation. Today's psalm starts right there. Somebody in the village says, we're going up to the house of the Lord, and the psalmist's heart jumps. Then, a few lines later, the pilgrims are standing inside the gates of the city they walked for days to reach. Today: I rejoiced.
screen: `LET'S GO.` → `THE HEART JUMPS.` → `STANDING INSIDE THE GATES.`

segments.voice: It's one of yesterday's gradual psalms, a road song, and it opens with joy. In the Douay-Rheims: "I rejoiced at the things that were said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord." First, the joy. Nobody is forcing anybody here. Going to worship is the good news, the thing you look forward to. Catholics sing this psalm at the start of Mass on Laetare Sunday, the Sunday of rejoicing in the middle of Lent, and it's used in the Liturgy of the Hours for feasts of Mary, who is sometimes called the house of God. Second, the arrival. The pilgrims stand inside the gates and look around at a city built close together, where the tribes come up to give thanks. A long road, and now: here. Third, the prayer. The psalm turns and asks for peace. In the words many English speakers know, from the King James: "Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: they shall prosper that love thee. Peace be within thy walls." In Hebrew there's a play on sounds. Peace is shalom, and Jerusalem is Yerushalayim, and the lines chime shalom, shalom, as if the city's own name held the word. Tradition has long heard it that way, though scholars aren't sure that's where the name comes from. Today Jerusalem is holy to Jews, to Christians, and to Muslims, and people of all three pray for its peace. The psalm doesn't say whose peace. It just asks for peace inside the walls, and for the ones who love the city.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: peace for a city. Settle, and breathe. Picture Jerusalem: stone walls, narrow streets, people of three faiths walking past each other every morning. Hold the people there who are grieving or afraid. If you pray, you can say the psalm's line: pray for the peace of Jerusalem. If you don't, simply wish peace to the people who live there, and then to one home you know where peace is thin. The bell holds the time.
I rejoiced. The first words of a pilgrim psalm: glad to be invited into the house of the Lord, and praying for the city's peace. Today's word.
Your line: peace within thy walls. Today, whatever walls you live inside, a home, a classroom, an office, do one thing that makes it a little more peaceful. Day one hundred eighty-five.

186.title: Unless the Lord build (Psalm 126 [127])
186.hook: they labor in vain that build without him
186.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 126 [127] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many begin the day with a morning offering, a traditional prayer that offers the day's work, joys and sufferings to God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I rejoiced: pilgrims inside Jerusalem's gates, praying for its peace. Your line was peace within thy walls. What did you do to make your walls more peaceful? Day one hundred eighty-six.

It's eleven at night. The laptop is still open. There's one more email, one more fix, one more thing, and you tell yourself if you just push a little longer, it'll all hold together. The coffee's cold. Tomorrow you'll get up early and do it again. Almost everyone knows that loop, the feeling that everything depends on you and you alone, and that if you stop for a second, it all falls down. Three thousand years ago, someone wrote a psalm for exactly that person. Today: unless the Lord build.
screen: `ELEVEN AT NIGHT, STILL WORKING.` → `IT ALL DEPENDS ON ME.` → `A PSALM FOR THAT PERSON.`

segments.voice: Another of the gradual psalms, and the heading gives it to Solomon, the king who built the Temple. It opens with two pictures. In the Douay-Rheims: "Unless the Lord build the house, they labour in vain that build it. Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it." First, notice what it doesn't say. It doesn't say don't build. It doesn't say fire the watchman. The builder still lays bricks, and the guard still stands on the wall. The psalm is about who the work finally rests on. Second, the tired worker. The next verse says it's vain to rise before dawn and stay up late, eating the bread of sorrow. And then comes a line that sounds almost too gentle for the Bible. In the King James: "for so he giveth his beloved sleep." Rest isn't laziness here. It's trust, the thing you can do when you know you aren't holding the whole house up alone. Third, the house. In Hebrew, house can mean a building and also a family, a household, a line of children. So the psalm goes on to children as a gift from the Lord. Build a home, raise a family, run a city: the psalm says all of it rests on God first. The Latin opening, Nisi Dominus, was set to music by Vivaldi and Monteverdi, and it's carved as a motto over doors and on city arms. Catholics also have an old habit that fits it well: the morning offering, a prayer at the start of the day that hands over all the day's work before it begins.
screen: `TWO PICTURES: BUILDER AND WATCHMAN.` · `STILL BUILD. STILL WATCH.` · `HE GIVETH HIS BELOVED SLEEP.` · `HOUSE MEANS FAMILY TOO.` · then, large: `UNLESS THE LORD BUILD THE HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer today's work before you start. Settle, and breathe. Name the main thing you'll work on today: a project, a shift, homework, looking after someone. See yourself starting it. Now, if you pray, hand it over: this is yours, Lord, before it's mine. Catholics often use the morning offering for this. If you don't pray, simply set an intention: I'll do my part, and I won't carry the whole house alone. The bell holds the time.
Unless the Lord build. The first words of a psalm that says our work, our cities and our families rest on God, not on our effort alone. Today's word.
Your line: not in vain. Today, do your work well, and then, tonight, stop. Go to sleep without finishing everything. Day one hundred eighty-six.

187.title: Out of the depths (Psalm 129 [130])
187.hook: the psalm prayed for the dead
187.howItsDone: Catholics pray the De profundis for the dead, in the Office of the Dead, at funerals and gravesides, and especially in November; it is also prayed at Night Prayer on Wednesdays in the Liturgy of the Hours.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unless the Lord build. Your line was not in vain. Did you manage to stop, and sleep, with something left undone? Today is a quieter psalm. Go gently. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

Some nights you're not on the road anymore. You're at the bottom of something. A diagnosis. A funeral. A mistake you can't take back. A phone call at three in the morning. Words run out. You can't manage anything polished or brave. Down there, people have reached for the same short psalm for well over two thousand years. Monks sang it at evening prayer. Families say it at gravesides. A famous writer's letter from prison was published under its first two Latin words. Today: De profundis.
screen: `AT THE BOTTOM OF SOMETHING.` → `WORDS RUN OUT.` → `ONE SHORT PSALM.`

segments.voice: It opens at the lowest point. In the Douay-Rheims: "Out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord: Lord, hear my voice." In Latin, De profundis clamavi ad te, Domine. First, the depths. In the Bible the deep waters are chaos and drowning, the place where your feet can't touch. The psalmist is in over his head, and he says so. The prayer doesn't wait until he's feeling better. It starts from the bottom. Second, the turn. The next thing he says is about sin, and it's disarmingly honest: "If thou, O Lord, wilt mark iniquities: Lord, who shall stand it." If God kept a ledger, nobody would last. Then comes the hinge: with God there is forgiveness. That's why this is one of the seven penitential psalms. Third, the waiting. The psalm doesn't end with rescue. It ends with hope that keeps going around the clock. In the Douay-Rheims: "My soul hath hoped in the Lord. From the morning watch even until night, let Israel hope in the Lord." The Hebrew pictures a watchman on the wall, waiting for dawn. Anyone who has sat up with someone sick knows that watch, waiting for the window to go gray. Fourth, the dead. Because it cries from the depths and hopes for mercy, the Church took this psalm as its prayer for those who have died. It's sung in the Office of the Dead, and for centuries Catholics have prayed the De profundis for the souls of the faithful departed, often at graves, often in the evening. Catholics believe the prayers of the living can help the dead on their way to God.
screen: `STARTING FROM THE BOTTOM.` · `IF YOU KEPT A LEDGER, WHO COULD STAND?` · `WAITING FOR THE MORNING.` · `THE CHURCH'S PSALM FOR THE DEAD.` · then, large: `OUT OF THE DEPTHS I HAVE CRIED TO THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: remember someone who has died. Settle, and breathe slowly. Let one person come to mind: a grandparent, a friend, someone you never got to say goodbye to. See their face. Remember one ordinary thing about them, the way they laughed, what they always cooked. If you pray, you can pray the first line of the psalm for them: out of the depths I have cried to thee, O Lord. If you don't, keep a quiet minute in their memory. The bell holds the time.
De profundis. Latin for out of the depths: the first words of the psalm the Church prays for the dead. Today's word.
Your line: out of the depths. Today, if you hit bottom in some small way, don't wait to feel better before you speak. The psalm starts from there. Day one hundred eighty-seven.

188.title: Like a weaned child (Psalm 130 [131])
188.hook: three verses about a quieted soul that doesn't grasp at great things
188.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 130 [131] in the Liturgy of the Hours, and many use it for quiet prayer, repeating its short verses slowly as a way of resting in God.

segments.voice: Yesterday, De profundis: the cry from the depths, prayed for the dead. Your line was out of the depths. Who did you remember? Today, the psalm right after it, and it's very quiet. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

Watch a hungry baby for thirty seconds. Everything is wanting. Crying, reaching, grabbing at the one thing that will make it better, right now. Then watch a toddler a year or two later, sitting on a parent's lap after a long day. Not grabbing. Not asking for anything. Just leaning back, heavy and content, because being held is enough. Those are two very different ways to be a child. And one of the shortest psalms in the Bible, three verses long, says a soul can learn the second one. Today: like a weaned child.
screen: `A HUNGRY BABY: ALL WANTING.` → `A TODDLER ON A LAP: CONTENT.` → `A SOUL CAN LEARN THAT.`

segments.voice: It's another gradual psalm, headed as David's, and it starts by letting go of ambition. In the Douay-Rheims: "Lord, my heart is not exalted: nor are my eyes lofty. Neither have I walked in great matters, nor in wonderful things above me." First, notice who's talking. The heading gives it to a king. Somebody with every reason to grasp at great things is saying: I've stopped. I don't need to understand everything or run everything. Second, the picture. The Douay's wording is hard to follow here, so listen to the King James: "Surely I have behaved and quieted myself, as a child that is weaned of his mother: my soul is even as a weaned child." Weaned is the key. In the ancient world, children often nursed until two or three. A nursing baby on its mother's lap wants one thing and cries until it gets it. A weaned child can sit on the same lap and want nothing, only the closeness. The Hebrew word is gamul. So the psalm isn't praising a soul that feels nothing. It's a soul that has stopped demanding, and is content to be held. Third, notice the mother. The image of God here is a parent's lap, and the psalmist is the child in it. Catholic writers have long loved this psalm for that tenderness, and Saint Thérèse's little way, which we met back in the saints, breathes the same air. Then the psalm ends by turning the whole people toward hope in the Lord, now and forever. Three verses. You can pray it in thirty seconds, and spend a lifetime learning it.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit like a child held. Settle into your chair and let it take your full weight. Let your hands open in your lap. Notice what you're reaching for today, the answer, the outcome, the thing you want to happen, and for two minutes, don't reach. If you pray, you can rest in God the way a child rests on a parent's lap, wanting nothing but to be there. If you don't, just rest in being held up by the chair and the floor. The bell holds the time.
Like a weaned child. A child who no longer demands, content simply to be held: the psalm's picture of a quiet soul. Today's word.
Your line: quieted. Today, when you catch yourself grasping at something you can't control, put it down for one breath and be quieted. Day one hundred eighty-eight.

189.title: By the rivers of Babylon (Psalm 136 [137])
189.hook: exiles weep, and the last verse is raw rage; the Church keeps it honest, not as a command
189.howItsDone: Catholics pray Psalm 136 [137] in the Liturgy of the Hours without its final verses, and read the whole psalm in scripture as the lament of the exiles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, like a weaned child: a soul content to be held. Your line was quieted. What did you put down? Today the quiet breaks. This one is raw. Day one hundred eighty-nine.

You may know the tune. A reggae song from 1970, later a disco hit, that half the world has sung at weddings without thinking about the words. The words are from a psalm. And the psalm is not a party. It's a group of refugees sitting beside foreign rivers, far from home. Their city has been burned. Their Temple is gone. And the soldiers who marched them there are standing over them saying: go on, sing us one of your happy songs from home. Today: by the rivers of Babylon.
screen: `A SONG FROM THE RADIO.` → `REFUGEES BY FOREIGN RIVERS.` → `SING US ONE OF YOUR SONGS.`

segments.voice: First, the history. In 587 before Christ, the Babylonian army destroyed Jerusalem and its Temple, and carried many of its people away to Babylon. This psalm is their voice. In the Douay-Rheims: "Upon the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept: when we remembered Sion." They hang their harps on the willows. Then the taunt comes, and their answer: "How shall we sing the song of the Lord in a strange land?" Second, the vow. If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, the psalmist says, let my right hand forget its skill. Jews have carried that vow for more than two thousand years, and at many Jewish weddings a glass is broken to remember Jerusalem in the middle of joy. Third, the ending, which is hard to hear. The last verse curses Babylon, and blesses whoever would take its little ones and dash them against the rock. There's no softening it. It's the rage of people whose own children were killed. So what does the Church do with that? It doesn't pretend the verse isn't there. It keeps it in the Bible as an honest cry, not as a command. The psalmist doesn't do it; he hands his rage to God. In the daily Liturgy of the Hours, the Church leaves those last verses out of common prayer. And some of the old monks read them another way: Saint Benedict, in his Rule, says to dash your evil thoughts against Christ, the rock, while they're still small. So the psalm teaches something surprising: the Bible lets people bring even their worst anger into prayer.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring your anger honestly. Settle, and breathe. Let yourself notice one thing you're angry about. Something done to you, or to someone you love, or something in the news. Don't dress it up. Name it plainly, in your head. If you pray, you can hand it to God as it is, rough and unfinished, the way the psalmist did. If you don't pray, just let yourself feel it without acting on it, and breathe out slowly. The bell holds the time.
By the rivers of Babylon. The song of exiles weeping for Jerusalem, whose last verse is rage handed over to God. Today's word.

Today, when anger comes, say it to God or to the quiet before you say it to anyone else. Day one hundred eighty-nine.
